newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-ORIOLES PROTEST OF FAN-ASSISTED HOMER DENIED.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-ORIOLES PROTEST OF FAN-ASSISTED HOMER DENIED.

text.p: Major League Baseball officials Friday denied a Baltimore Orioles protest of the New York Yankees home run that was assisted over the wall by the outstretched glove of a 12-year-old fan during Game 1 of their American League championship series.

The Major League Executive Council voted unanimously after careful consideration to support the decision of American League President Gene Budig to deny the protest filed by the Baltimore Orioles, officials said in a statement issued shortly before the third game of the series.

Orioles owner Peter Angeles had asked acting commissioner Bud Selig to direct Budig to reverse the umpire's decision, based on quotes by umpire Rich Garcia that he had erred in not calling fan interference on the critical play.

The Orioles had argued that it was in the best interest of baseball to nullify the New York victory and replay the game from the point in the eighth inning before Derek Jeter's long fly ball made young Jeffrey Maier the toast of New York.
Baltimore was winning 4-3 before Jeter's controversial homer tied the game, later won by the Yankees on an 11th-inning homer by Bernie Williams.

"The best interests power of the commissioner does not apply in this case," Selig said. "It is not intended to be used to circumvent the onfield judgment of the umpires or the express authority of the league presidents to decide game-related protests."

The decision sent to Angelos said Garcia's ruling was an instantaneous call that did not violate any playing rule and that it was not relevent that Garcia was later quoted admitting that he had called the play incorrectly.

"In case of a judgment call, post-game statements or quotations attributed to umpires by the press cannot form the basis for overturning the result of a game and replaying it from a certain point," the decision said.
"Apart from the chilling effect it would have on umpires, such a rule would create havoc for all involved."
